Summary
Stiff leg syndrome (SLS) is considered as a focal form of stiff
person syndrome (SPS) in which symptoms are confined to
a distal limb. A patient with stiff leg syndrome developed a
malignant neuroleptic syndrome (NMS) after having been
treated with a single dose of haloperidol. She developed
renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation,
and died despite extensive treatment. The potential vulner-
ability of patients with SPS/SLS to NMS is discussed.

Case Report
An 35-year-old woman presented to hospital due to pain-
ful spasms of her both legs, causing walking problems and
frequent falls. 6 years ago, due to progressive stiffness and
painful spasms of right leg elicited by leg movements and
emotional, auditory or tactile stimuli, presence of high titer
of anti-GAD 65 antibodies in her serum, and the typical
electrophysiological findings, she had been diagnosed as
SLS in another hospital. She had been prescribed clonaze-
pam 2 mg twice daily and her symptoms had been initially
improved substantially. About one year ago, her symptoms
came back and gradually evolved to both legs. During
the two months prior to her admission her symptoms had
become very severe. She was admitted to the hospital to
adjust the treatment.
On admission, she was well oriented and cooperative.
There were no signs of truncal rigidity or exaggerated
lumber lordosis. Both of the legs were rigid and painful.
Sudden tactile and auditory stimuli triggered spasms of the
legs. Motor examination of the legs could not be evaluated
because of the stiffness of the legs. Vibration sense was
reduced distally in the lower extremities. Motor and sensory
examinations were normal on the rest of the body. Patellar
jerk was hyperactive, but deep tendon reflexes on the upper
limbs were normal.
She have type | diabetes and her blood glucose was
poorly controlled despite insulin treatment. Her past medi-
cal history was remarkable for a diagnosis of hyperthyroi-
dism 15 years ago. She used propylthiouracil for 1 year
and remained euthyroid afterwards. She was diagnosed
with depression 6 months ago and started on venlafaxin.
Her daily medication on admission included clonazepam
(2 mg x 2), venlafaxin (75 mg x 1) and NPH insulin.
Blood chemistry examination revealed hyperglycemia
(203 mg.dL). Renal, hepatic function, electrolytes, chest-
X ray, electrocardiogram and urinalysis were normal. The
erythrocyte sedimentation rate was: 6 mm.h'!. Serum cerulo-
plasmin, copper, and B12 levels were within normal limits.
Insulin dosage was increased according to blood glucose
level. Magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the thoracic and
lumbar spine, and electroencephalogram were normal.
In the second day of hospital admission, she was given
5 mg of i.m. haloperidol for agitation. 5 mg of i.m. diazepam
was given due to painful spasms of her legs, 2 hours after
haloperidol administration. About 5 hours after haloperi-
dol administration, she had tremulousness and her speech
became dysarthric. Her temperature rose to 40.3 °C. She
was hypertensive (180/110 mmHg) and tachycardic (140/
min). Laboratory investigation revealed leukocytosis (leu-
kocyte count 21.1K.4~L"). Biochemical work-up showed:
glucose: 196 mg.dL"', K:6.5 mEg.L', SGOT: 30 U.L",
SGPT: 62 U.L', LDH:422 U.L', CK:1295 U.L'with nor-
mal CK MB fraction and cardiac troponin levels. Arterial
blood samples while breathing room air: pH:7.31, pO2:80.6
mmHg, pCO>:20.6 mmHg, standart HCO2:14.1 mmol.
L", base excess:-13.7 mmol.L. The levels of TSH, FT3
and FT4 were within normal limits. The insulin dose was
readjusted and the patient received vigorous hydration,
diuretic, and i.y. NaHCOs to alkalinize the urine and to
decrease potassium level. A lumbar puncture was per-

formed. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was clear and showed
no abnormalities. Blood, urine, CSF, and sputum samples
were collected for culture and she was started empirically
on ceftriaxone 2 g i.v. once daily. An electroencephalogram
showed diffuse slow waves consistent with encephalopathy.
MRI of the brain was normal. Cooling blankets and ice packs
were used to decrease temperature. Venlafaxin was stopped
and no further neuroleptic medication was used. The patient
was observed for the night. The next day, the patient had a
Glasgow coma score of 11, she developed lead pipe rigidity
and her elevated temperature persisted (38.5 °C), Her blood
pressure was labil. Her platelet count dropped down to 24K.
»L" (her initial platelet count was 271 K.wL"'). Prothrombin
time was borderline elevated, but the partial thromboplastin
time was normal as were levels of fibrinogen and D-dimer.
CK level climbed to 6845 U.L", SGOT level was 428 U.L",
SGPT level was 215 U.L"', and LDH level was: 422 U.L!
Urine myoglobin was positive. C-reactive protein value
(CRP) level was: 1.52 mg.L". Using serologic tests with the
following pathogens could be excluded: hepatitis A, B and C
virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein Barr virus, human immune
deficiency virus, and herpes simplex virus 1. Antinuclear
antibody (ANA), anti-ds DNA, extractable nuclear antigen
(ENA) and RF were within normal limits. With the above
findings, the diagnosis of NMS was suggested and she was
transferred to the intensive care unit. Bromocriptin was ini
ated a dosage of 2.5 mg three times a day and was in ed
to 10 mg four times a day gradually. Because of abnormal
liver function test results, dantrolen sodium was not given.
Later that same week, the cultures came back negative.
A day later, she required intubation and ventilatory sup-
port for acute respiratory failure. A chest x-ray showed
marked fluid overload. Tracheal aspirate culture was nega-
tive. Continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF)
was instituted due to oliguria, remarkable fluid accumula-
tion, exacerbated azotemia, and hyperpotasemia. Urine
myoglobin level was 1370 ng.mI' and the serum CK level
peaked at 104.136 U.L'. She developed complete anuria.
On the 3th day after the administration of haloperidol, the
antibiotic treatment was changed to piperacillin/tazobactam
2.25 g iv. every 8 hours, despite negative culture results.
Total parenteral nutrition was started. SGOT and SGPT lev-
els peaked at 3210 and 1892 U.L" respectively on the 5 th
day. Then, levels of CK, SGOT and SGPT started to decrease
and dropped down to 511, 54, and 69 U.L" respectively on
the 16 th day. Her trombosit level started to increase and
peaked at 231 K.wL’! on the 15 th day. However, her acute
renal failure did not improve and she remained anuric until
death. Coagulase-negative s. haemolyticus was isolated
from blood culture on the 11th day and it was considered
as indicative of contamination. Nevertheless, it was sensi-
tive to piperacillin/tazobactam which she used to take. She
developed overt disseminated intravascular coagulation on
the 19 th day after haloperidol administration, and despite
treatment, died four days later.

This patient met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of
Mental Disorders, Fourth Revision (DSM-IV) criteria for
NMS [2].

Our patient had some of the risk factors such as younger
age, poor controlled diabetes mellitus, and parenteral use of
high potency antipsychotic (haloperidol).

No signs of autonomic hyperactivity were observed in
our patient before the cerastropiie process, but they might
have been overlooked. Altogether, disturbance of inhibitory
GABA-ergic pathways in SLS may have made the patient
more vulnerable to neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It
remains to be investigated. The present rigidity, spasms and
agitation might also have contributed to the development of
clinical picture of severe NMS in our patient.
